title: From a table to a rule
objectives: Find the rule of a function from a table of its values
Undo a function to find the input for a given output

screens.prose: A machine's rule is hidden. You can only watch what goes in and what comes out.
screens.question: What comes out when 5 goes in?

hints.text: How much does the output grow from one row to the next?
The outputs read 4, 7, 10, 13.
Each row adds 3 to the output, so the next is $13 + 3 = 16$.

feedback.correct: The outputs climb by 3 each row, so 13 becomes 16.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how the output column changes from row to row.

byKey.add-one: You added 1 because the input went up by 1. The output column climbs by 3 each row.
byKey.doubled: You doubled 13. The outputs go up by adding the same amount each row, not by doubling.

explain.text: The outputs climb by 3 each time the input climbs by 1. So the next output is 16. A steady climb like this is the first clue to the rule.

screens.prose: Here are those rows as points: input across, output up. The two sliders set a rule: multiply by one number, then add another. Its line moves as you slide.

derive.caption: Your rule: multiply by {{a}}, then add {{b}}

screens.question: Set the sliders so the line passes through all four points. Which rule did you make?

options.why: You used the climb of 3 as the number added. Check input 2: $2 + 3 = 5$, not 7.
This fits the first row only. Input 2 gives 8, not 7.
You used the first output, 4, as the number added. Input 1 then gives 7, not 4.

hints.text: Start with the first slider. Which setting makes the line as steep as the points?
The points climb 3 for each step across.
Multiply by 3, then try adds until the line hits (1, 4): add 1.

feedback.correct: Multiply by 3, then add 1, hits all four points.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test your rule on every row, not just one.

explain.text: Only multiply by 3, then add 1, hits every point. The 3 is the climb per row. The 1 is the output at input 0, one step back from 4.

canvas.caption: Your rule: multiply by 3, then add 1

screens.prose: You found two numbers. The climb per row is what the rule multiplies by. The output at input 0 is what it adds. So that machine was $f(x) = 3x + 1$.
screens.question: Write the rule for this table: $f(x) = \ldots$

hints.text: How much do the outputs climb per row?
The row with input 0 gives the number added.
Climb 4 and start 5: $f(x) = 4x + 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the climb per row, then the output at input 0.

byKey.swapped: You swapped the two numbers. Check input 0: $5 \times 0 + 4 = 4$, but the table says 5.
byKey.climb-added: You used the climb of 4 as the number added. Input 2 would give 6, not 13.

explain.text: The outputs climb by 4, so the rule multiplies by 4. Input 0 gives 5, so it adds 5. Check the last row: $4 \times 3 + 5 = 17$.

screens.prose: This time the inputs do not go up in ones.
screens.question: Which rule fits every row?

options.why: You used the climb of 6 as the multiplier, but the input climbs by 2. Check $x = 3$: $6 \times 3 - 1 = 17$, not 11.
This fits the first row only. At $x = 3$ it gives 7, not 11.

hints.text: How much does the input climb per row? And the output?
The inputs go up in 2s.
The output climbs 6 for an input climb of 2: that is 3 per 1. Then $5 = 3 \times 1 + 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the output climb by the input climb.

explain.text: The output climbs 6 when the input climbs 2, so 3 for each 1. Row 1 then fixes the number added: $5 = 3 + 2$. The multiplier is always output climb over input climb.

screens.prose: Another hidden rule. Check the climbs before you predict.
screens.question: What is $f(6)$?

hints.text: Do the outputs climb by the same amount each row?
0, 1, 4, 9, 16: compare each output with its input.
Each output is the input times itself: $f(x) = x^2$, so $f(6) = 36$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The climbs change, so look for another link between input and output.

byKey.next-row: 25 is $f(5)$, the next row. The question asks for input 6.
byKey.last-climb: You kept adding the last climb, 7. The climbs grow, 1, 3, 5, 7, so the outputs do not lie on a straight line.

explain.text: The climbs are 1, 3, 5, 7, so no single multiplier fits. Each output is the input squared: $f(x) = x^2$. Then $f(6) = 36$. This is the edge case: a table whose climb is not constant.

screens.prose: Back to $f(x) = 3x + 1$. This time you see an output, 31, and want the input. Running a machine backwards like this is called undoing it.
screens.question: What input gave 31?

hints.text: Which step did the machine do last? Undo that one first.
Undo "add 1" by subtracting 1: $31 - 1 = 30$.
Then undo "multiply by 3" by dividing: $30 \div 3 = 10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the steps in reverse order: the last step first.

byKey.forward: You ran the machine forwards on 31. We want the input that gives 31.
byKey.wrong-order: You divided by 3 first, then subtracted 1. Undo the last step first: subtract 1, then divide.
byKey.add-back: You added 1 instead of subtracting it. To undo adding 1, take 1 away.

explain.text: You undid the steps in reverse order: subtract 1, then divide by 3. Check: $f(10) = 31$. The undoing is itself a rule: input $y$ gives $\dfrac{y - 1}{3}$.

screens.prose: Another hidden rule. A colleague looks at the first two rows and says it doubles the input.
screens.question: What is $f(4)$?

options.why: You used $f(x) = 2x$, which fits the first two rows only. It gives $f(3) = 6$, but the table says 8.
You added the last climb, 4, again. The climbs double too: 2, then 4, so next 8.

hints.text: Check the colleague's rule on every row, not just the first two.
Does doubling 3 give 8?
Each output is double the one before: 2, 4, 8, so the next is 16.

feedback.correct: Each output doubles the one before, so $f(4) = 16$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test the rule on the third row.

byKey.doubles-x: You trusted a rule that fits two rows. $2x$ predicts $f(3) = 6$, and the table says 8.

explain.text: A rule that fits two rows can still fail the third. Here each output doubles the one before, so $f(4) = 16$. Always test a rule on every row.

screens.prose: Here is what you did each time. When the inputs climb in equal steps and the outputs do too, $$m = \frac{\text{output climb}}{\text{input climb}}, \qquad f(x) = mx + c$$ Find $c$ from any one row, then check the rule on every row.
screens.question: Inputs 2, 4 and 6 give outputs 1, 7 and 13. What is $m$?

hints.text: The outputs climb 6 between rows. How much do the inputs climb?
The inputs climb 2, so $m = \tfrac{6}{2} = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the output climb by the input climb.

byKey.climb: 6 is the output climb. The inputs climb by 2 at the same time, so divide by 2.
byKey.upside-down: You divided the input climb by the output climb. The output climb goes on top.

explain.text: Each row the output climbs 6 while the input climbs 2. So the output rises 3 for every 1 of input: $m = 3$.

screens.prose: Now finish that table's rule. Inputs 2, 4 and 6 give outputs 1, 7 and 13.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: The output climbs 6 per input climb of 2, so $m = 3$
Check row 3: $3 \times 6 - 5 = 13$, as the table says

hints.text: You need $m$ before you can find $c$.
Finding $c$ uses one row and the value of $m$.
Find $m$, then $c$, then write the rule, then check it.

feedback.correct: Multiplier, then the number added, then the rule, then a check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.c: Finding $c$ needs $m = 3$ already, so the climb line comes first.
byKey.check: A check tests a finished rule, so it comes last.

explain.text: $m$ comes from the climbs, and $c$ from one row once $m$ is known. The rule $f(x) = 3x - 5$ then has to pass every row. Row 2 also works: $3 \times 4 - 5 = 7$.

screens.prose: You hold 40 shares bought at £15.25 each. The table gives your profit, $P(s)$, at three final prices $s$.
screens.question: Which rule gives $P(s)$, in pounds?

options.why: This leaves out what you paid. At £16.00 it gives £640.00, not £30.00.
This is the profit on one share. At £16.00 it gives £0.75, not £30.00.
You used the £60.00 climb between the last two rows, but the price climbed £1.50 there. Per £1 it is £40.00.

hints.text: How much does the profit climb for each £1 on the final price?
From £15.00 to £16.00 the profit climbs £40.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the climb per £1 of price, then use one row.

explain.text: Each £1 on the price adds £40.00, one pound per share. Then $c = 30 - 40 \times 16 = -610$, which is minus the £610.00 the shares cost. So $P(s) = 40s - 610 = 40(s - 15.25)$.

ideas: A table lists a function's inputs and outputs; the rule is what links every row.
For steady climbs, $m$ is the output climb over the input climb, and $c$ comes from any one row.
To undo a function, reverse its steps, last step first.

formula.name: A rule from a table
formula.tex: m = \dfrac{\text{output climb}}{\text{input climb}}, \qquad c = f(x_1) - m x_1
formula.note: Then check $f(x) = mx + c$ on every row.

summary.trap: A rule that fits two rows can fail the third. Test every row.

options.why: The outputs fall by 2 each row, so the multiplier is −2, not 2.
You swapped the two numbers. Input 0 gives −2 with this rule, but the table says 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the output at input 0 and the climb per row.

explain.text: Input 0 gives 7, so $c = 7$. The outputs fall by 2 each row, so $m = -2$. The rule is $f(x) = 7 - 2x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the last step first.

byKey.forward: You ran the machine forwards on 25. We want the input that gives 25.
byKey.wrong-order: You divided by 4 first, then added 3. Undo the last step, subtracting 3, first.
byKey.wrong-way: You subtracted 3 again. To undo subtracting 3, add 3.

explain.text: The machine multiplied by 4, then subtracted 3. Undo in reverse: $25 + 3 = 28$, then $28 \div 4 = 7$. Check: $4 \times 7 - 3 = 25$.

feedback.correct: The climbs are 3, 5, 7, so the next is 9: $18 + 9 = 27$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how the climbs themselves change.

byKey.last-climb: You added the last climb, 7, again. The climbs grow by 2 each time.

explain.text: The climbs 3, 5, 7 grow by 2, so the next climb is 9 and $f(5) = 27$. The rule is $f(x) = x^2 + 2$: $25 + 2 = 27$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the output climb by the input climb first.

byKey.climb-m: You used the climb of 10 as the multiplier. The input climbs by 5, so $m = 2$.
byKey.next-row: 32 is $f(15)$, the next row. Input 20 is two rows on.

explain.text: The output climbs 10 while the input climbs 5, so $m = 2$. Input 0 gives 2, so $c = 2$. Then $f(20) = 40 + 2 = 42$.
